title: India–EU

cards.b:
The European Union is India's largest trading partner in goods (with the US), a top investor and a source of technology. Yet for decades the relationship was called an 'underperforming partnership'. In 2026 that changed, at least on paper.

In January 2026, at the 16th India–EU summit in New Delhi, the two sides announced the conclusion of a Free Trade Agreement after nearly two decades of off-and-on talks. EU leaders (Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa) were chief guests at Republic Day 2026.

The exam angle: why is Europe now more attractive to India, what are the hurdles, and how does the EU fit into India's multi-alignment?

The 2004 partnership and the 2005 Joint Action Plan set broad aims, but results were thin. India found the EU slow and bureaucratic. The EU found India protectionist.

The FTA talks (the Broad-based Trade and Investment Agreement) began in 2007 and stalled in 2013 over cars, wine and spirits, services visas, and data protection. The Porto summit (May 2021) and the 2022 relaunch restarted them, together with separate talks on investment protection and geographical indications.

• Trade: about €120 billion in goods in 2023-24, plus large services trade. The EU is India's biggest export market in some years.
  • Technology: the India–EU Trade and Technology Council (TTC), set up in 2022, covers semiconductors, AI and digital standards. India is only the second TTC partner after the US.
  • Connectivity: the 2021 Connectivity Partnership, the Global Gateway, and IMEC (2023).
  • Climate and energy: green hydrogen, solar and the International Solar Alliance.
  • Security: maritime cooperation, counter-terrorism, and Indo-Pacific engagement. The EU adopted an Indo-Pacific strategy in 2021.

Individual members matter too. France has been a strategic partner since 1998 and sells the Rafale. Germany builds submarines with Indian yards (a Project 75I partnership with Mazagon Dock was in progress in 2025–26). Italy, Spain and Netherlands are growing partners.

The agreement was concluded on 27 January 2026. As of the latest reports (autumn 2026), it still needs legal scrubbing, formal signing and ratification by both sides, including the European Parliament and the EU Council. Check the latest status before the exam.

  • Industrial goods: big tariff cuts both ways. India lowers duties on cars, wines and spirits in phases, with quotas.
  • Services and mobility: the two sides also agreed to work on easier movement of professionals and students.
  • Protected areas: sensitive farm items like dairy are largely kept out.
  • Rules: chapters on sustainability, services, digital trade and intellectual property.

Europe called it a huge deal covering two billion people. India framed it as a way to hedge against US tariff shocks.

• CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism): the EU's carbon tax on imports of steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser and others started its definitive phase in January 2026. India says it is unfair to developing countries and violates 'common but differentiated responsibilities'.
  • EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR): compliance costs for Indian farm goods.
  • Data and digital rules: the EU does not give India 'data adequacy' status.
  • Russian oil: the EU sanctioned Nayara in 2025 and banned imports of refined fuels from Russian crude from 2026. This hits Indian refiners exporting to Europe.
  • Values: European Parliament resolutions criticising India on human rights, for example on Manipur in 2023, irritate Delhi.
  • Pace: the EU's ratification process is slow and can be contested by member states and farm lobbies.

EU policy is made in Brussels, but many results come from individual capitals.

  • France: strategic partner since 1998. It sold 36 Rafale jets (2016), then 26 Rafale-M for the Navy (agreed 2025), and builds Scorpene submarines in Mumbai. Its support at the UN Security Council has been steady. The Horizon 2047 roadmap (2023) sets long-term goals. France is also in the Indo-Pacific through its overseas territories.
  • Germany: India's biggest European trade partner. It is working on a submarine project (Project 75I) and is a G4 partner for UN reform.
  • Italy, Netherlands, Nordics: technology, shipping, green energy.

Brexit also pushed the UK to build a separate track, which led to the 2025 CETA.

The war in Ukraine split Europe and India. Europe saw a threat to the rules-based order. India saw a European war and kept buying Russian oil. In June 2022 Jaishankar told a European audience that Europe must stop thinking its problems are the world's problems, a line widely quoted.

Over time Europe accepted India's position and began to see it as a swing power. In 2024–25, European leaders courted India for trade and defence deals. In 2026 the concluded FTA shows how far this has come.

Still, Europe watches closely: refined fuels from Russian crude, sanctions on Nayara and the future of S-400 purchases are tests of trust.

Optimists see Europe as a partner that, unlike the US or China, has no territorial quarrel with India and no appetite to arm Pakistan heavily. Sceptics recall that two decades of 'imminent' deals went nowhere.

Scholars such as Garima Mohan and Jagannath Panda argue Europe needs a bigger security role in the Indo-Pacific, while India needs a clear sense of what it wants from the EU beyond trade.

India's other recent FTAs show the pattern: EFTA TEPA (signed March 2024, in force October 2025, with a $100 billion investment pledge over 15 years) and the India–UK CETA (signed July 2025).

• Use the FTA to bring exports of textiles, leather, gems, pharma and engineering into a market of 450 million consumers.
  • Seek EU technology in semiconductors, green steel and defence co-production.
  • Negotiate carbon rules (CBAM) in line with the Paris Agreement.
  • Link with Europe in IMEC and Indo-Pacific security (EU naval missions, port calls).
  • Treat France, Germany and Italy as bridges to the EU level.

For an Indian student of IR, the lesson is simple. A middle-power India benefits from diversified partners. The EU, Japan and the Gulf are not alternatives to the US. They are insurance against US unpredictability.

"Critically examine the prospects of an India-EU FTA." (typical)
"Why is the EU important for India's foreign policy and economy?" (typical)
"Assess the impact of CBAM on India's trade." (typical)

Structure: (1) background: 1994, 2004, 2007–13, 2022; (2) pillars: trade, technology, connectivity, security; (3) the January 2026 FTA and its status; (4) friction: CBAM, EUDR, data, Russian oil; (5) assessment; (6) way forward: ratify, align standards, link to IMEC and Indo-Pacific.

Mention France and Germany to show you know the member-state layer.

India–EU FTA negotiations (BTIA) first started in:
quiz.w: Talks began in 2007 and stalled in 2013.

quiz.q: The India–EU FTA was announced as concluded at the summit held in:
quiz.w: At the 16th India-EU summit, New Delhi, 27 January 2026.

quiz.q: India is only the second partner, after the US, with which the EU set up a:
quiz.w: The EU-India TTC was set up in 2022.
It taxes the carbon content of selected imports into the EU.

quiz.q: The EFTA–India TEPA entered into force in:
quiz.w: Signed 10 March 2024 and in force from 1 October 2025.

quiz.q: The India–EU Connectivity Partnership was launched at the summit in:
India's main objection to the EU's CBAM is that it:
o: Imposes costs on developing countries, against common but differentiated responsibilities
quiz.w: India argues it ignores the CBDR principle and burdens developing economies.

quiz.q: Which sector is largely kept out of the FTA because of sensitivity?
quiz.w: India protected dairy and some farm sectors.
